A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MM-DeceptionBench and the debate with images framework. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures support comparison despite extensive reformatting and relocation.

before.justification: V1 reports original human-annotated evaluations, comparisons across three benchmarks, ablations, computational measurements, and case studies.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds overall and category-specific deception rates for 13 models in Table 1.

M1.justification: The sequential debate, assigned stances, visual operations, evidence reconstruction, judge, and utility equation remain unchanged. Algorithm 1's notation corrections and the revised explanation of the utility's two explicit terms clarify the existing procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same six-category MM-DeceptionBench, comprising 1,013 cases and 1,096 images, alongside PKU-SafeRLHF-V and HallusionBench's Visual-Dependent subset. Additional evaluated model backbones do not establish new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Direct prompting, CoT prompting, majority voting, and debate about images retain the same participation in the three-benchmark comparison across four backbones (v1 Table 2; v2 Table 3). The new leaderboard concerns target-model characterization.

E3.justification: V2 expands model characterization to 13 backbones, including Gemini-3, Qwen3, and Claude-4.6 variants. Sections 3.1 and B.2.3 also revise labeling eligibility to require convergent behavioral evidence, including alternative-prompt checks, and exclude reasoning-answer inconsistency, whereas v1 Section 5.1 accepts reasoning-output misalignment. This materially revises the reported protocol without establishing that retained results were rerun or relabeled.

E4.justification: The agent/round sensitivity evidence changes in v2 Figure 4a, and the full stance-ratio accuracy series from v1 Figure 6 is omitted. Other tool ablations, case studies, category-wise errors, and failure analyses are retained; v2 Appendix F largely reorganizes v1 Appendix E.5.

E5.justification: Neither version reports benchmark confidence intervals, significance tests, or seed-level variability. The three samples used for majority voting and the reported human-annotation agreement statistics remain unchanged.

E6.justification: V2 Table 1 newly reports overall and six-category deception rates for 13 models, including overall rates of 88.1% for Gemini-2.5-Pro and 15.9% for GPT-5. Figure 4a also changes plotted detection rates: two agents and three rounds move from 78.4% in v1 Figure 4 to approximately 86.5%. The matched judge-performance, three-benchmark, ablation-grid, cost, and confusion tables retain their numerical values.

T1.justification: Remark 4.2 newly concludes that the debate game is incentive-compatible from the evidence-cost asymmetry; v1 only states that deception is asymmetrically costlier. This adds a theoretical assertion without a new proof. Equations (1)-(6), the information-retention assumption, and Appendix A's proof are unchanged.

C1.justification: The benchmark novelty, improved human agreement, and transfer claims remain. V2 adopts an explicitly functional account of deception and narrows the conclusion's deployment framing from scalable inference-time monitoring to offline auditing rather than real-time filtering.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands the interpretation of deception through reward-driven strategic misalignment, observable evidence rather than inferred intent, and distinctions between deceptive omission and ordinary promotional emphasis. It explicitly treats chain-of-thought as potentially unfaithful, adds explanations for unilateral judges' failures, and discusses model/category variation. Most appendix failure-mode explanations already existed in v1.

D1.justification: V2 newly explains enforcing the cost parameter through soft prompting or budget constraints and explicitly states that Annotator Remarks are withheld from evaluated models. Prompt templates, inference parameters, hardware requirements, and computational measurements remain. The dataset, code, and project hyperlinks also retain their destinations despite different display text.

R1.justification: V2 adds focused references supporting its conceptual boundaries and visual-ambiguity discussion, including Hubinger et al., Grice, Chisholm and Feehan, and Chen et al. It removes the Virgil reference and GPT-4.1 announcement. The central positioning against textual deception benchmarks and prior debate research remains.

P1.justification: The abstract and substantial introduction, dataset-specification, and conclusion passages are rewritten. Experimental discussion separates characterization from detection, while appendices are reorganized into dedicated implementation, judge-evaluation, and limitations sections with a new contents page. These are substantial narrative and structural changes.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column main-text layout, replaces Figure 1, adds the leaderboard, and redraws and consolidates v1 Figures 4-6 into one three-panel figure. The stance plot becomes baseline-relative bars, tables are reformatted or relocated, and appendix case displays are enlarged and redistributed.

improvement.justification: V2 adds useful model-level prevalence evidence, clearer conceptual boundaries, and better organization. However, its revised labeling exclusions are not reconciled with retained cases and results, and the redrawn ablation introduces numerical conflicts: Figure 4a shows kappa about 0.52 for two agents and three rounds, while unchanged Table 6 reports 0.49. These unresolved reliability issues make the net quality benefit uncertain.
